Where is Charleston, SC, and how is the city laid out?

Charleston is the county seat of Charleston County and the most populous city in South Carolina. It sits on Charleston Harbor, which is formed by the Ashley, Cooper and Wando rivers and runs about 7 miles southeast to the Atlantic.

The old downtown is known as the Peninsula, with the Ashley River on the west and the Cooper River on the east. The city limits also take in West Ashley, James Island, Johns Island, the Cainhoy Peninsula and Daniel Island. A house on the Peninsula and a house on Johns Island share a city name but face very different rules, lot types and buyer pools.

What does Charleston's history mean for an older house?

Charleston has been settled for more than 340 years, so many houses here are old, and old houses come with repair lists. The city was founded in 1670, and by the 1690s it was among the five largest cities in North America.

Two events left marks on the building stock. An earthquake in 1886, estimated at magnitude 7.0, damaged about 2,000 buildings. Hurricane Hugo, a Category 4 storm on September 21, 1989, caused more than $2.8 billion in damage.

Neither event decides what your house is worth today. They do explain why buyers and inspectors in Charleston look closely at foundations, roofs, wiring and past water damage, and why a seller with deferred repairs may find a traditional listing slow.

What drives the Charleston economy?

Charleston's economy rests on tourism, port and logistics, aerospace and information technology. The Port of Charleston is one of the busiest in the country, and Boeing is a major aerospace employer.

The technology sector has grown enough to earn the nickname Silicon Harbor. Education adds to the mix: the College of Charleston and The Citadel are both in the city.

For a seller, this mix means demand comes from several directions at once: people relocating for jobs, investors, and buyers who want a second home near the water. It also means a house in the wrong condition or the wrong flood zone can be hard to place with an ordinary buyer who needs a mortgage.

How do hurricanes and flooding affect selling a house in Charleston?

Flood risk is the single biggest condition issue for many Charleston houses. The city sits at about 3 feet of elevation, summer is the wettest season with almost half of the annual rainfall falling from June through September, and hurricanes are a threat in summer and early fall.

The City of Charleston runs a floodplain program with rules that matter at sale time. Its Flood Zones page says any work inside a Special Flood Hazard Area needs a permit, including painting, interior finishes and storm-damage repairs. The Special Flood Hazard Area covers AE, Coastal A and VE zones, which have a 1 percent or greater annual chance of flooding.

The city's floodplain page lists these points for owners:

  • Since July 1, 2020, new construction in the flood hazard area must be designed 2 feet above Base Flood Elevation, and residential substantial improvements must be 1 foot above it.
  • Slab-on-grade building types 1A, 1B, 2A and 3 are prohibited in the 100-year floodplain for projects applied for on or after January 1, 2024.
  • Coastal A Zone design rules have applied to new construction and substantial improvements since January 1, 2023.
  • FEMA's Risk Rating 2.0 applied to new flood policies from October 1, 2021 and to renewals from April 1, 2022.

Elevation certificates and flood hazard information can be requested from the city at floodplain-info@charleston-sc.gov. Ask for them before you set a price, because a buyer's flood insurance quote can change what they are willing to pay. See the city's floodplain management page and flood zone permit page.

Can a buyer run a short-term rental in a Charleston house?

Only in limited cases. The city sorts short-term rentals into categories by location, and every category limits a property to one short-term rental unit.

  • Category 1 covers the Old and Historic District on the peninsula, for existing structures individually listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
  • Category 2 covers the rest of the peninsula outside the overlay, for buildings constructed 50 or more years ago.
  • Category 3 covers areas off the peninsula, including Daniel Island, James Island, Johns Island and West Ashley.

Each category requires one extra off-street parking space, 9 feet by 18 feet 6 inches, on top of the parking the zoning ordinance already requires. A single-family home needs 3 spaces in total. Commercially zoned property in the overlay can seek a Commercial Short Term Rental Permit, and residentially zoned property can seek a Bed and Breakfast Permit. Questions go to shorttermrental@charleston-sc.gov or 843-724-7311. The details are on the city's category criteria page.

If your house has been used as a rental, tell buyers what permit it holds. A buyer paying for rental income will want proof.

What does it cost to transfer a deed in South Carolina?

The state deed recording fee is $1.85 for each $500 of value, or any part of $500, under South Carolina Code section 12-24-10. Of that, $1.30 goes to the state and $0.55 to the county.

The seller is the one liable, with the buyer secondarily liable. Taking a $300,000 sale as an example, there are 600 blocks of $500, so the fee works out to $1,110. A value affidavit is filed with the deed, and the register of deeds can waive it. Some transfers are exempt, including a deed in lieu of foreclosure, and the affidavit must then state the reason. The statutes are at scstatehouse.gov.

Charleston County sets its own recording and tax dates. We could not open the county auditor and assessor pages while writing this, so call those offices for the current reassessment notices, appeal dates and bill due dates before you plan a closing.

How is a house taxed in Charleston, and does that change when you sell?

South Carolina taxes an owner-occupied legal residence at a 4 percent assessment ratio, and other property at 6 percent. The 4 percent rate applies to the home and up to five contiguous acres, and the home cannot be rented for more than 72 days in a calendar year.

A buyer who will not live in the house usually loses the 4 percent rate, so the same house can carry a larger bill after a sale to an investor. Counties must reassess property every fifth year, and owners must be notified of value changes of $1,000 or more (Code sections 12-43-217 and 12-43-220).

What do sellers in Charleston usually face?

Sellers here tend to run into the same few problems, and each one points to a different sale route.

  • Flood-zone repairs that need a permit before they can start.
  • Older structures with deferred roof, plumbing or electrical work.
  • Inherited houses that need heirs to agree before anything is signed.
  • Rental houses where the tenant, the permit or both need sorting out.

A listing suits a house that is in good shape and can wait for showings. A sale to a cash buyer suits a house where repairs, permits or a deadline make a long listing a poor fit. Whichever you choose, get the flood zone, the permit history and your payoff figure in hand first.

More questions about Charleston, SC

What is the main flood rule when I sell a house in Charleston?

The city requires a permit for any work in a Special Flood Hazard Area, including repairs after storm damage. Since July 1, 2020, residential substantial improvements there must sit 1 foot above Base Flood Elevation. Ask the floodplain office for your elevation certificate before you price the house.

How much is the South Carolina deed fee on a Charleston sale?

It is $1.85 per $500 of value, so a $300,000 sale carries a $1,110 fee. By statute the seller is liable and the buyer is secondarily liable. Your closing attorney will show the exact figure.

Can I rent my Charleston house short term after buying it?

Maybe. Each of the city's three categories allows one short-term rental unit per property and an extra parking space. Category 1 and 2 depend on location and building age on the peninsula. Confirm with the city before you count on rental income.

Does selling to a cash buyer change flood or permit duties?

No. Disclosure, permits and the deed fee apply however the house sells. A cash sale can skip buyer financing delays and repair requests, and that is the practical difference for most Charleston sellers.

Where can I find Charleston County tax dates?

Start with the county auditor, assessor and treasurer. South Carolina law sets January 15 as the last day to pay without penalty on most bills, but the county notices and appeal windows are specific to each cycle, so call the offices directly.

Where is Columbia, SC, and what is special about its location?

Columbia is the capital of South Carolina and the county seat of Richland County, with parts of the city reaching into Lexington and Kershaw counties. It sits near the center of the state at the fall line, where the Piedmont meets the Atlantic Coastal Plain.

The Broad and Saluda rivers meet here to form the Congaree River. That geography shaped the city, and it still matters for anyone selling a house close to the water.

How did Columbia become the capital, and why does it matter for houses?

Columbia was South Carolina's first planned capital. The General Assembly approved the site on March 22, 1786, and surveyor John Guignard laid out a grid two miles on a side, five years before the plan for Washington, D.C.

Union forces under Sherman captured the city on February 17, 1865, and much of it burned that night and the next day. Modern historians conclude Sherman did not order the fire. The result is a city with a planned core, a mix of surviving and rebuilt neighborhoods, and housing from many eras.

That mix is why a Columbia seller can own anything from a historic bungalow to a postwar ranch. The condition issues differ a lot from one street to the next, so a buyer's price is rarely a citywide number.

Which neighborhoods and areas make up Columbia?

Columbia has many named neighborhoods, each with its own housing stock and buyer base. Names listed for the city include:

  • Arsenal Hill and Congaree Vista near downtown
  • Elmwood Park and Waverly Historic District
  • Five Points, Old Shandon and University Hill, close to the university
  • Granby Mill Village and Rosewood

Most of the city is served by Richland County School District One. Parts of the city that fall in Lexington or Kershaw counties are handled by those counties for property records, so check which county your parcel is in before you call an office.

What employers and institutions drive Columbia's housing demand?

State government, the University of South Carolina and Fort Jackson are among the largest employers in Columbia. The University of South Carolina is the state's flagship, with more than 30,000 students on the Columbia campus.

Healthcare and insurance add steady jobs through Prisma Health Midlands and BlueCross BlueShield of South Carolina. Manufacturing names include Michelin, Honeywell, Westinghouse Electric and FN Herstal. Allen University, Benedict College, Columbia College, Columbia International University and Midlands Technical College are also in the city.

Sellers of rental houses near the campuses or downtown should expect buyers to ask about tenants and rental permits, which the section on rentals below covers.

What is the weather like in Columbia, and what does it mean for a roof or HVAC?

Columbia has a humid subtropical climate with hot, humid summers and mild winters. The record high is 113 degrees Fahrenheit, set on June 29, 2012, and the record low is minus 2 degrees on February 14, 1899. Snow averages only about 1.2 inches a year.

Long, hot summers put the load on air conditioning, attic ventilation and roofing, so inspectors here pay close attention to those.

Because the city sits on the fall line, with rivers that meet downstream, ask for a flood zone determination on any parcel near the Broad, Saluda or Congaree rivers.

How do you get around Columbia, and why does it matter to a seller?

Columbia is served by four interstates: I-20 running east and west, I-26 running northwest to southeast, I-77 running north toward Rock Hill and Charlotte, and I-126 linking downtown to I-26 and I-20. Columbia Metropolitan Airport has service from American Eagle, Delta Connection and United Express, and Amtrak's Silver Star stops in the city daily.

A smaller airfield, Jim Hamilton-L.B. Owens Airport, handles general aviation in Rosewood. Good road access is a real selling point for a Columbia house, and a house near an interstate ramp or a rail line should be described honestly to buyers, since noise comes up in showings.

What rules cover rentals in Columbia?

Every residential rental in the City of Columbia needs a Residential Rental Permit before it is occupied as a rental. The requirement applies to units rented after July 1, 2016, and permits expire each year on December 31.

  • Owners of up to 4 units use the nonbusiness form, and owners of 5 or more use the business form.
  • Applications go to the Code Enforcement Division at 920 Hemlock Drive, Columbia, SC 29201, and payment is made online after approval.
  • The contact listed for questions is 803-545-4362.

Short-term rentals have their own rules. Operating one needs an STR Permit from Code Enforcement and a Business License. Under Ordinance 2025-107, STRs are allowed in mixed-use, activity center and corridor, commercial and employment campus districts. In residential districts they are allowed on parcels fronting a four-lane arterial or collector street. An ordinance approved March 3, 2026 lets owner-occupied homes in residential districts operate without the four-lane requirement. See the city's STR page and the residential rentals page.

How do property tax bills and appeals work for a Columbia house?

In South Carolina, county governments levy and collect property tax, and the Richland County Assessor sets values for houses inside Columbia. Taxes are due between September 30 and January 15, and penalties follow in steps: 3 percent after January 15, another 7 percent if still unpaid by February 2, and another 5 percent by March 17 (Code sections 12-45-70 and 12-45-180).

To contest a value in Richland County, file a written objection with the Assessor, online or in person, with documents that support your number. The deadline is 90 days from the dated reassessment notice, or the first penalty date on the current bill, whichever comes first. A representative needs a power of attorney on Form SC2848, and an LLC needs to provide its organizing documents.

The Assessor's Office is at 2020 Hampton Street, Suite 2058, Columbia, SC 29204, phone 803-576-2640. The county's assessment appeal page has the online portal. We did not find a confirmed reassessment year on that page, so ask the office.

What options do Columbia sellers have for a quick sale?

A Columbia seller can list with an agent, sell without one, or accept a cash offer. Houses near the university or downtown often attract investors, while houses in need of work or with tenants in place are harder to sell on the open market.

Before you decide, gather the permit status of any rental, the parcel's county, the tax bill, and your mortgage payoff. Those four items answer most of the questions a buyer or closing attorney will ask.

Is Columbia in Richland County?

Yes. Columbia is the seat of Richland County, but parts of the city extend into Lexington and Kershaw counties. Check your parcel's county before contacting an assessor or treasurer.

Do I need a rental permit to sell a rented house in Columbia?

The city requires a Residential Rental Permit for every rental unit, renewed each year by December 31. A buyer will want to see that it is current. Ask Code Enforcement at 803-545-4362 if you are unsure.

When are Richland County property taxes due?

State law makes taxes payable between September 30 and January 15. A 3 percent penalty follows after January 15, so ask the treasurer for your exact notice date and amount.

How long do I have to appeal a Columbia assessment?

Richland County allows 90 days from the dated reassessment notice, or until the first penalty date on the current bill, whichever comes first. Filing an appeal does not replace paying the bill.

Can a buyer use a Columbia house as an Airbnb?

Only if zoning and the city permit allow it. The city requires an STR Permit and a Business License. Residential locations depend on the street or on owner occupancy under the 2026 ordinance.

Where is North Charleston, SC, and which counties does it cover?

These numbers come from the city's Wikipedia entry. The three-county split is the first thing a North Charleston seller should sort out, because the county decides who assesses the property, who bills the tax and where the deed is recorded.

How did the Navy and Boeing shape North Charleston?

North Charleston grew around the Charleston Naval Shipyard, established in 1901, and the Naval Base that operated from 1902 to 1996. Voters approved incorporation in an April 27, 1971 referendum, and the city was incorporated on June 12, 1972. In 2010 the Air Force Base and the Naval Weapons Station merged into Joint Base Charleston.

Employers named in the city entry include:

  • Boeing, which chose North Charleston in October 2009 for a 787 Dreamliner assembly line.
  • Kapstone, with about 1,100 workers at its kraft paper mills.
  • InterContinental Hotels Group, with more than 400 call center workers.
  • iQor, with 360 workers, and Mercedes-Benz vans, with 200.

The Hugh K. Leatherman Terminal, a 280-acre container facility, opened its first phase in April 2021. Those worker counts come from the Wikipedia article and may be out of date, so treat them as a rough guide.

What is the weather like, and what flood questions come up?

North Charleston's weather record, taken at Charleston International Airport, shows average annual precipitation of 51.03 inches and about 2,809 hours of sunshine. The mean July high is 91.1 degrees, the mean January low is 37.5 degrees, and snowfall averages just 0.5 inches a year. Those are 1981 to 2010 normals.

The bigger risk is water. Hugo in September 1989 caused more than $2.8 billion in damage across the Lowcountry. Charleston County's flood flyer advises homeowners to learn their flood zone, flood depth and flood history, because standard homeowners insurance generally does not cover flood damage.

  • A flood policy typically starts 30 days after purchase.
  • A house in a Special Flood Hazard Area with a federally backed mortgage must carry flood insurance.
  • Premiums depend partly on elevation, and an agent may request an elevation certificate.

If a prior owner raised the house or elevated its equipment, that paperwork helps a buyer's insurer, so gather it before you list.

Which schools and transport links do North Charleston buyers ask about?

North Charleston is served by two school districts, Charleston County School District and Dorchester School District Two, and the right one depends on the address. High schools named in the city entry are North Charleston High, R.B. Stall High, Academic Magnet High, Military Magnet Academy and Fort Dorchester High, which is in Dorchester District Two. Higher education includes Charleston Southern University, Trident Technical College and ECPI University.

Getting around, according to the same entry:

  • Charleston International Airport serves more than 2.9 million passengers a year.
  • Amtrak, Norfolk Southern and CSX provide passenger and freight rail.
  • CARTA runs the city bus system.
  • A planned intermodal center would combine a train station, long-haul bus service and CARTA at one site.

The entry does not name specific interstates, so check a map for exits near your house. Ask a local agent how commute to the airport, port or base affects your street.

Which North Charleston neighborhoods have the oldest housing?

Park Circle was one of the first areas planned in 1912, with industrial, commercial and residential sections. When the city incorporated, it took in Russelldale, Ferndale, Morningside, Liberty Park, Palmetto Heights, Singing Pines, Dewey Hill, Liberty Homes and John C. Calhoun Homes.

The city's parks include Riverfront Park and Northwoods Park, as well as Park Circle itself. Older neighborhoods can have aging wiring, plumbing and roofs, and repair costs are something a financed buyer's inspector will raise. A cash sale does not require you to make those repairs first.

The city's own pages list a Code Enforcement department, Business Licenses, Zoning with an online map, Building Inspections and a Certificate of Occupancy page. We could not open the detail pages, so for a rental, a vacant house or an open violation, call City Hall at 843-554-5700 at 2500 City Hall Lane before you list.

How do North Charleston property taxes and assessments work?

The county that holds your parcel assesses it, so the part of North Charleston in Charleston County uses the county's rules, and parcels in Berkeley or Dorchester follow those counties. We confirmed the Charleston County details only, so ask the other two offices about their dates.

In Charleston County, the county FAQ puts a primary residence at a 4 percent assessment ratio and other real estate at 6 percent. Tax equals assessed value times millage, and one mill is one thousandth of a dollar. Owners who live in the house apply for the 4 percent legal residence status, and the county recommends filing early in the year.

State law makes taxes payable between September 30 and January 15, with penalties of 3, 7 and 5 percent that start after that date, as set out in Chapter 45. Reassessment notices went out in August 2025 with an appeal deadline of November 18, 2025, per a notice from a nearby town. Properties sold or transferred are an exception to the 15 percent cap.

The county Auditor handles real estate questions at (843) 958-4234 or RealProperty@CharlestonCounty.org.

What happens at closing, and what about inherited or landlord-owned houses?

Charleston County parcels are recorded at the Register of Deeds, 101 Meeting Street, Suite 200, Charleston, open 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. on weekdays, phone (843) 958-4800. The state's deed fee is $1.85 per $500 of value, and estate distribution deeds are excluded under Chapter 24.

For disclosure, Title 27, Chapter 50 requires a written statement from an owner unless the sale is exempt. Transfers by a fiduciary administering an estate, guardianship or trust are exempt, which is useful if you are an executor selling a parent's home. The law also allows as-is deals.

The city entry reports that North Charleston had the highest eviction filing and judgment rate among U.S. cities of 100,000 or more as of 2016. Landlords with problem tenants may therefore find a cash sale of an occupied house worth comparing with listing it.

A fiduciary administering an estate is exempt from the written disclosure statement under South Carolina law. Heirs who sell in their own names may not be, so confirm with an attorney.

  • The Old Village, the oldest neighborhood, centered on the Pitt Street Shops. The Mount Pleasant Historic District is on the National Register of Historic Places.
  • Scanlonville, one of the first African American communities formed after the Civil War, now annexed into the town.
  • Riverside, which opened in 1930 and is now a gated community.

If you own an older home near the Old Village, ask the Town of Mount Pleasant's planning staff whether exterior repairs need review before you spend money. We could not confirm the town's review rules from an official page, so we leave the specifics to that office.

How does flood and storm risk change a Mount Pleasant home sale?

Flood risk is the first thing many Mount Pleasant buyers and their lenders check, because the town sits low and borders tidal water. Hurricane Hugo came ashore at Sullivan's Island in September 1989 with an eight-foot surge at Charleston, and one death in Mount Pleasant came from the rising Cooper River, according to the Hugo summary.

Charleston County's flood flyer lists the practical points that show up at closing:

  • A standard homeowners policy generally does not cover flood damage, so flood coverage is a separate policy through the National Flood Insurance Program or a private carrier.
  • A home in a Special Flood Hazard Area with a federally backed mortgage must carry flood insurance.
  • Flood policies typically take effect 30 days after purchase.
  • An insurance agent may ask for an elevation certificate, which a surveyor, engineer or architect can prepare if the town has none on file.

The county flyer gives its own building office number for unincorporated areas and some towns, and says other towns have separate numbers. Call the Town of Mount Pleasant to ask which flood zone a parcel is in and whether an elevation certificate is already on file. A seller who has that paper in hand removes a delay.

Which schools, bridges and roads matter to Mount Pleasant buyers?

Public schools in Mount Pleasant belong to the Charleston County School District, and buyers often ask about the school zone first. The town entry lists these among its public schools and transport links:

  • Wando High School, which opened in 1973, plus Lucy Garrett Beckham High School and Oceanside Collegiate Academy.
  • Middle schools named Laing, Moultrie and Thomas Cario.
  • The Arthur Ravenel Jr. Bridge, an eight-lane cable-stayed span that opened July 16, 2005 and carries U.S. 17 across the Cooper River to Charleston.
  • Charleston International Airport, about 12 miles northwest, and Mount Pleasant Regional Airport (Faison Field) inside the town limits.

School zones are set by the district, so check the district's address lookup rather than relying on a listing description. Commute times over the bridge matter to many buyers, but we do not quote traffic figures because we found no official count.

How is a Mount Pleasant deed recorded, and what does recording cost?

A deed for a Mount Pleasant house is recorded with the Charleston County Register of Deeds at 101 Meeting Street, Suite 200, in Charleston. The office is open Monday through Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., and does not take walk-in documents for recording after 4:30 p.m. The phone number is (843) 958-4800. The office says it cannot help you fill out forms.

South Carolina charges a deed recording fee of $1.85 for each $500 of value or fraction of $500. That is $1.30 for the state and $0.55 for the county, under the state code. As an illustration, a $500,000 sale works out to $1,850. The county's own flat recording charges are listed in a fee schedule on its site.

Some transfers are exempt, including deeds of distribution from a decedent's estate and quitclaim or corrective deeds that confirm title the grantee already holds with no payment. An affidavit stating either the value or the reason for the exemption goes with the deed.

When are Mount Pleasant property taxes due, and what happens when you sell?

Charleston County bills Mount Pleasant property taxes, and state law makes them payable between September 30 and January 15. If they are unpaid after January 15, a 3 percent penalty applies, with another 7 percent added if still unpaid before February 2 and another 5 percent before March 17.

The county FAQ says a primary residence is assessed at 4 percent of market value and other real estate at 6 percent. A buyer who will not live in the house, or a seller who has moved out, should expect the higher ratio to matter for who pays what at closing.

The most recent countywide reassessment notices went out in August 2025, and the appeal deadline was November 18, 2025, according to a notice posted by a neighboring town. Most properties are protected by a 15 percent cap on taxable value increases, but sold or transferred property is an exception, so a buyer's bill can differ from the seller's.

Contacts at the county Auditor: real estate at (843) 958-4234 and homestead exemption questions at (843) 958-4200, option 4. A new owner files their own legal residence application. Filing early in the year, before bills are mailed, is the county's own advice.

What must a Mount Pleasant seller disclose?

An owner who sells a house in South Carolina generally gives the buyer a written property condition disclosure on the form set by the Real Estate Commission. The owner may state what they know about each listed condition or state that they make no representation about it.

A knowing false or misleading disclosure can make the owner liable for actual damages, court costs and possibly attorney fees. The statute also leaves room for as-is sales: nothing in it prevents parties from agreeing on the property's condition. Some transfers are exempt, including those by a fiduciary administering an estate, a foreclosure, and a transfer where both sides agree in writing to skip the statement.

The details are in Title 27, Chapter 50. For a specific situation, ask a South Carolina real estate attorney.

Do I need flood insurance to sell a Mount Pleasant house?

The seller does not buy a policy to sell, but a buyer with a federally backed mortgage on a house in a Special Flood Hazard Area must carry flood insurance. Flood policies usually take 30 days to start, so a financed buyer should ask early.

Can I sell my Mount Pleasant house as-is?

Yes. South Carolina's disclosure law does not stop an as-is agreement, though you still may owe the buyer the disclosure statement unless your transfer is exempt.

Call the Charleston County Auditor at (843) 958-4234 for real estate bills, or (843) 958-4200, option 4, for the homestead exemption.

Where is Rock Hill, and what is it like for someone selling a house?

It sits in the Piedmont along the Catawba River, and its northern edge runs to Lake Wylie. The city covers roughly 44 square miles, according to Wikipedia, and it is the largest city in the county.

For a seller, that location matters in a simple way. Charlotte is close enough that a Rock Hill seller should expect buyers to look at homes on both sides of the state line. A house with a tired kitchen, an old roof or a stack of deferred repairs has to compete with all of them, and a long repair list is often what slows a traditional sale down.

How did Rock Hill grow, and who employs people there now?

Rock Hill grew around the railroad and then around textile mills. The Charlotte and South Carolina Railroad brought the first passenger train on March 23, 1852, and the town later served as a rail transfer point during the Civil War. Textiles dominated the local economy for generations. When mill jobs moved overseas, the city shifted toward manufacturing, retail and recruiting new companies.

Wikipedia lists these among the larger employers in the city:

  • Comporium Communications
  • Hyosung Corporation

  • Winthrop University

The area has also seen serious storms. Roofs, trees near the house and drainage are the usual trouble spots after storms like these. York County sends one tax notice per year to the owner of record as of January 1, and real estate taxes can be paid without penalty from September 30 through January 15. Because of that rule, a notice can arrive in the seller's name even after a sale, which is why the county tells people to ask their closing attorney how to handle the year of transfer.

State law adds the late penalties. Under S.C. If back taxes sit on your Rock Hill house, they are usually paid out of the sale proceeds at closing.

  • Inoperable or unregistered vehicles cannot sit outside unless they are in a garage or carport.
  • Exteriors are checked for rotted boards, sagging roofs, peeling paint and damaged porch steps or railings.
  • Interior items include wiring, plumbing, windows and doors, smoke alarms and pest control.

For overgrown grass or debris, the city issues one notice per year starting January 1, and a second offense goes straight to a ticket or court summons. The York County notice goes to whoever owned the property on January 1, so the bill may still carry your name after closing. The county says to ask the closing attorney how the year of transfer is handled, and taxes are usually split between buyer and seller on the settlement statement.

For a seller, the size matters in one practical way. Sumter is a mid-sized city with a county seat's worth of offices in one downtown, so deeds, tax bills and city permits are all handled by offices in the same downtown.

What is Sumter's history, in brief?

Sumter was incorporated as Sumterville in 1845 and shortened to Sumter in 1855, named for General Thomas Sumter of the Revolutionary War. The surrounding Sumter District was created in 1798 and became Sumter County under the 1868 Constitution.

The city adopted the council-manager form of government on June 11, 1912. In September 2024 the National Park Service named Sumter and Sumter County a joint World War II Heritage City.

The older parts of town include the Sumter Historic District and the Stateburg Historic District. The city also has a Design Review Board, so if your house is in an older district, ask the planning office whether exterior changes need review.

Spartanburg began as a courthouse village in the 1780s and was incorporated in 1831. Cotton mills began operating in 1816, and around 40 textile mills had been established by the early 1900s.

Hilton Head Island is a barrier island in Beaufort County, in the South Carolina Lowcountry, about 20 miles northeast of Savannah, Georgia. Everything about a sale here is shaped by the fact that it is an island: the bridge, the tides, the gates and the water.

The Town's total area is 69.13 square miles, but only 41.35 of that is land. The island is shaped like a shoe, with about 12 miles of Atlantic beachfront, and Broad Creek separates an older northern section from a younger southern one. Soils outside the tidal marsh are sandy.

What is the history of Hilton Head Island in brief?

The island is named for Captain William Hilton, who identified a headland near Port Royal Sound in 1663. Native Americans lived there for thousands of years before that, and Spanish explorers arrived in 1521.

Confederate Fort Walker fell to more than 12,000 Union troops on November 7, 1861, and the island became a major base for the blockade of Southern ports. Hundreds of freed people settled there during the war, and many of their Gullah descendants still live on the island.

Modern development began in the 1950s. The James F. Byrnes Bridge opened in 1956, the same year Charles E. Fraser started Sea Pines. A four lane bridge replaced the old swing bridge in 1982, Cross Island Parkway opened in January 1997, and the Town was incorporated after a May 1983 referendum.

Tourism drives the economy. About 2.5 million visitors come each year, and the population can reach roughly 150,000 in peak summer. Golf is a major draw: the RBC Heritage, a PGA Tour event, is played at Harbour Town Golf Links in Sea Pines.

Where is Bluffton, South Carolina?

Bluffton is a town in southern Beaufort County, mainly along US 278 between Hilton Head Island and Interstate 95. It is part of the Hilton Head Island metropolitan area, though Jasper County, which shares that area, does not contain the town.

The town covers 54.19 square miles, of which 51.97 are land, which makes it the fifth-largest municipality in South Carolina by land area. The 2020 census counted 27,716 residents, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 36,807. The May River runs through the center of town and the New River forms its southwest boundary.

For a seller, the layout has a quirk. Strict state annexation laws left unincorporated pockets, called doughnut holes, inside the town limits. A house with a Bluffton address may therefore sit under county rules and not town rules, so check which applies before you assume anything about permits or rental licenses.

What is Bluffton's history?

Bluffton was settled in 1728 and incorporated in 1852. The original one-square-mile core, now called Old Town, sits on a bluff above the May River, on land once home to the Yamasee.

The Bluffton Movement of 1844 protested federal taxes and is tied to the early secession push in South Carolina. On June 4, 1863, Union forces destroyed about two-thirds of the town's roughly 60 structures. Old Town was named a National Historic District in 1996, and the Heyward House became the town's welcome center in 2000.

Bluffton Oyster Company opened in 1899, and galleries line Calhoun Street today.

How fast has Bluffton grown, and what does that mean for sellers?

Very fast. Bluffton's population grew 882.7 percent from 2000 to 2010 and another 121.2 percent from 2010 to 2020. Planned developments from the early 2000s housing boom drove much of it, and the Sun City Hilton Head community and 1990s growth on Hilton Head Island had already revived commercial activity in town.

Several of those developments stayed partly unfinished after the Great Recession. That history means a Bluffton house can sit in a community with a homeowners association, a master plan or amenities still under development.

  • Ask the association for its governing documents and any unpaid dues before you sign a contract.
  • Check whether your lot is inside the town limits or in a doughnut hole.
  • Collect any plat, survey and permit records you have, since the county's recording rules ask for a legal description or a reference to a recorded plat.

Bluffton's median age was 40.5 in the 2020 census, and tourism and higher education are both part of the economy.

How do hurricanes and flooding affect a Bluffton house?

Bluffton is in South Carolina's Southern Coastal Hurricane Region, and Beaufort County has a single evacuation zone, so an evacuation order applies to the whole county. The Bluffton Township Fire District, at (843) 757-2800, points residents to the state's official zone maps at Hurricane.SC and a town evacuation routes PDF.

The climate is humid subtropical, with mild winters and hot, humid summers. August is the wettest month, and the yearly total is about 50.4 inches. Buyers in a coastal county reasonably ask about wind and water, so it helps to gather the roof age, past claims and any flood paperwork you have.

The elevation is only about 20 feet. We could not open a town flood map page, so ask the Town of Bluffton or Beaufort County which flood zone your lot is in rather than relying on a listing.

Do Bluffton's short-term rental rules affect a sale?

They can, if the house is used as a rental. Town Ordinance 2023-248, adopted May 15, 2023, regulates short-term rentals, which it defines as renting a residential dwelling for fewer than 30 days.

  • Operating a short-term rental business requires a license from the Town Clerk, unless an exemption is granted.
  • A license runs one calendar year and must be posted where it can be seen at the property.
  • The clerk can suspend, revoke or decline to renew a license for good cause.
  • A person affected can appeal to the Town Manager within 10 days of written notice, and then to Town Council within 10 days. The council's decision is final.

A buyer of a rental will ask whether the license is current and whether the home sits inside the town. Ask the town about a license transfer on the main line, 843-706-4500, because the ordinance text we read does not say what happens at a sale.

How does property tax work for a Bluffton seller?

Beaufort County reassessed in 2023 and its next reassessment is scheduled for 2028. State law requires a reassessment every five years.

A primary residence is assessed at 4 percent of appraised value if the owner applied, and other residential and commercial property at 6 percent. The county's Important Dates page gives January 1 through January 15 of the following year for the 4 percent application, and the same window for an objection to value, or within 90 days of an assessment notice. You cannot use both options in one tax year.

A sale is an assessable transfer of interest. The appraisal date is December 31 of the year of transfer, and the new value applies for the following tax year. The county's transfer exemption can reduce the market value by up to 25 percent, but not below the current county record, and the application is due before January 31. Questions go to the Assessor at (843) 255-2400.

Tax is payable through January 15, with state penalties of 3 percent from January 16, another 7 percent after the second of February and another 5 percent after March 17.

What does recording a deed in Beaufort County involve?

Deeds are recorded at the Beaufort County Register of Deeds, 100 Ribaut Road in Beaufort, open 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Monday through Friday. The phone is (843) 255-2555.

The county's checklist is detailed. A deed generally needs a return-to name and address, two witnesses who are not parties to the deal, a notary block, a legal description, the grantee's address, a district, map and parcel number and a derivation clause. Warranty deeds also need a preparation clause.

The county lists a flat $15 deed fee plus the state and county fee of $1.85 per $500 of the price, as of August 1, 2019. Hilton Head Island has an extra transfer fee, and it applies only to certain district numbers. Three e-recording companies are accepted, and documents received after 4:30 p.m. are processed the next business day.

South Carolina requires an attorney to supervise the closing. Ask them to confirm the current fees.

More questions about Bluffton, SC

Is Bluffton, SC in Beaufort County or Jasper County?

Beaufort County. Jasper County is part of the same metropolitan area but does not contain the town of Bluffton.

Does Bluffton require a license to rent a house short term?

Yes. Town Ordinance 2023-248 requires a short-term rental license from the Town Clerk for rentals of fewer than 30 days, unless an exemption is granted. Licenses run for one calendar year.

When is Beaufort County's next reassessment?

The county says 2028, after its last reassessment in 2023. State law requires one every five years.

Does a sale raise the property tax on a Bluffton house?

It can. A sale is an assessable transfer of interest, so the home is reappraised as of December 31 of that year. The new value applies the next tax year, and a transfer exemption may reduce it by up to 25 percent.

Does Beaufort County evacuate by zone?

No. The county has a single evacuation zone, so an order covers the whole county.

Where is Aiken, South Carolina, and how is it laid out?

Aiken is the county seat and largest city of Aiken County, about 20 miles northeast of Augusta, Georgia. US 1 and US 78 run through town, and Interstate 20 passes about 6 miles to the north, reached by SC Highway 19 at exit 18 or US 1 at exit 22.

The city covers 21.58 square miles. The 2020 census counted 32,025 residents, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 33,808. The median age was 47.6, and 29.3 percent of residents were 65 or older.

An older population means estate sales and downsizing moves are a normal part of the local picture, and both can leave a house to sell with a tight timeline.

What is Aiken's history, and why does it still matter for houses?

Aiken was incorporated on December 19, 1835, around the end of a rail line running from Charleston to the Savannah River. It is named for William Aiken, the first president of that railroad.

In the late 1800s wealthy families from the Northeast began spending winters here, and Thomas Hitchcock Sr. and William C. Whitney helped found the Aiken Winter Colony. That legacy explains the horse culture. The Aiken Training Track, the Aiken Thoroughbred Racing Hall of Fame and Museum (founded 1977) and the Aiken Steeplechase Association (founded 1930) are all part of town life. The Imperial Cup runs in March and the Holiday Cup in October.

It also explains the older housing stock. Hopelands Gardens and the roughly 2,100 acres of Hitchcock Woods sit inside the city, and older homes around them may fall under the exterior review rules described below.

The Savannah River Site is the biggest single influence. The Atomic Energy Commission announced the site near Aiken on November 30, 1950, and it was renamed the Savannah River Site in 1989. Savannah River Nuclear Solutions, a Fluor and HII partnership, manages and operates it.

How do Aiken's weather and roads affect an older house?

Aiken has a humid subtropical climate with hot, humid summers and cool, dry winters, and it is milder than much of the state. Rainfall averages about 51 inches a year, and snow averages only about half an inch. The record high is 109 degrees (August 21, 1983) and the record low is minus 4 degrees (January 21, 1985).

With that much rain and heat, roofs, crawl spaces and cooling systems tend to draw attention on an older house. A buyer's inspector will look at roofs, crawl spaces, HVAC age and moisture, and a long repair list can slow a conventional sale.

Public schools are part of the Aiken County Public School District, and the city's high schools include Aiken High, South Aiken High and Silver Bluff High.

Does Aiken have historic district rules that affect a seller?

Yes, if your address is in a review area. Aiken's Design Review Board reviews Certificate of Appropriateness applications, and the city sets two filing deadlines.

  • Complex projects need an application 30 days before the board meets. That covers new construction, demolition, additions, relocations, porch enclosures and work touching more than one exterior historic feature.
  • Simpler projects need an application 14 days before a meeting. That list includes non-in-kind window, door or siding replacement, fences, gutters, handicap ramps, painting, paving and screening a porch.

If you plan to renovate before listing, the review calendar can add weeks. If you sell as-is, the buyer inherits the question, so the seller does not wait on it. The Planning Department at 803-642-7608 can tell you whether an address falls under the review, and it can give you the board's meeting schedule, which the city page we opened does not list.

What does South Carolina require when you sell an Aiken house?

Most sellers of a one to four unit home must hand the buyer a written property condition disclosure statement. It covers water and sewer, structure, mechanical systems, wood-destroying insects, zoning, environmental hazards such as lead paint and radon, leases and homeowners association rules.

Some transfers are excluded from the disclosure rule.

  • Court-ordered transfers and foreclosure-related transfers.
  • Transfers by a fiduciary, such as an estate representative.
  • Transfers to a spouse or lineal relative.
  • Sales where both sides agree in writing not to complete the form.

State law also allows an as-is agreement, and it says the buyer remains responsible for inspecting the property. A seller who knowingly gives false or incomplete information can be liable for actual damages and court costs.

The closing is overseen by a South Carolina attorney, because the State Bar treats every stage of a real estate transaction as the practice of law. The attorney prepares the deed, runs the title work and records the deed in the Aiken County Register of Deeds office.

Deeds for Aiken property are recorded at the Aiken County Register of Deeds, in the Government Center at 1930 University Parkway, Suite 2100. The phone is 803-642-2072.

The office keeps records back to 1872. Documents recorded after June 12, 2005 are imaged and can be viewed on computers in the office, and earlier documents are kept in book form. The state deed recording fee is $1.85 for each $500 of the price, and the county retains $0.55 of each $1.85.

The county page does not list a fee table, so ask the office or your closing attorney for the full recording total on your deed.

How does property tax work when you sell in Aiken?

Aiken County property tax is billed once a year, and state law sets the calendar. Taxes are payable from September 30 through January 15. Late penalties then step up: 3 percent from January 16, 7 percent more after the second of February, and 5 percent more after March 17.

An owner-occupied home is assessed at 4 percent of value if the owner applied for the legal residence rating, and other residential property is assessed at 6 percent. A sale is a reappraisal event, so the buyer's bill can differ from yours.

Sellers who are 65 or older, disabled or legally blind may already have the state homestead exemption of the first $50,000 of value. For the Aiken County assessor and treasurer details, see our Aiken County property tax guide.

Usually yes. South Carolina requires a written disclosure statement for most sales of one to four unit homes, with listed exceptions such as fiduciary and foreclosure transfers. An as-is sale is allowed, but a false statement can still create liability.

Does Aiken have a historic district review for exterior changes?

Yes. The Design Review Board reviews Certificate of Appropriateness applications, with filing deadlines of 30 days for complex projects and 14 days for simpler ones before a meeting.

At the Aiken County Register of Deeds, 1930 University Parkway, Suite 2100. Call 803-642-2072 to confirm requirements. Your closing attorney normally handles the recording.

Where is Mauldin, SC, and what is around it?

Mauldin is a city in Greenville County, South Carolina, south of the county's center and between Greenville to the northwest and Simpsonville to the southeast. It is part of the Greenville-Anderson-Greer metropolitan area.

The city covers about 12.13 square miles, almost all of it land, at an elevation of about 906 feet. U.S. Route 276 (Main Street) runs through the center, 8 miles to Greenville and 5 miles to Simpsonville. Interstate 385 follows the eastern side of the city, north to Interstate 85 and south to Interstate 185, and I-185 continues about 13 miles west-northwest to I-85 on the southwest side of Greenville.

Mauldin takes its name from a railroad. Benjamin Griffith received the first land grant in the area in 1784, and in 1885 Lieutenant Governor W. L. Mauldin helped bring the Greenville and Laurens Railroad through the village. The station was named Mauldin, and the name spread to the surrounding community.

The Civil War left the community nearly depopulated, and it did not fully recover until after World War II. The city's population was 22,889 in 2010 and 24,724 in the 2020 Census, which made it the 19th most populous city in South Carolina. The Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 31,465.

Where is Anderson, South Carolina?

Anderson is the county seat of Anderson County, in the northwest corner of South Carolina on the Piedmont plateau. It sits roughly at the midpoint of the Interstate 85 corridor, about 120 miles from Atlanta and 140 miles from Charlotte, and about an hour from the Blue Ridge Mountains.

The city is compact. It covers 15.86 square miles at an elevation of 738 feet. The 2020 census counted 28,106 people in 11,282 households, which made it the 16th most populous city in the state. The Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 31,323, and the median age is 36.6.

Why is Anderson called the Electric City?

William C. Whitner started electric service in 1895 from a hydroelectric plant on the Rocky River, and the city became one of the first in the Southeast with power. It was also the first in the world to run a cotton gin on electricity.

The Portman Dam washed away in 1901, which left the city dark until it was rebuilt in 1902. How did Conway get its name and its start?

The town was founded in 1732 under Royal Governor Robert Johnson's Township Scheme, on a bluff above the Waccamaw. Colonists called it Kings Town, and the name later became Kingston. Horry County was created in 1801 with its courthouse in Kingston.

The name then changed to Conwayborough, honoring General Robert Conway, and in 1883 the General Assembly renamed it Conway. A river town with that history has older blocks near downtown and newer subdivisions farther out, and the two sell differently.

Downtown revitalization began with the Main Street USA project in the 1980s, and the Riverwalk along the Waccamaw is now a restaurant district. Houses within walking distance of it are the ones sellers tend to mention first.

Conway's anchors are Coastal Carolina University, county government and a handful of industrial employers. Named employers include New South Companies (a Canfor subsidiary), Vulcan Materials Company and AVX Corporation.

The Grainger Generating Station, a Santee Cooper coal plant, ran from 1966 until it retired in 2012. Horry-Georgetown Technical College and a Webster University branch also operate in the area, and most of the county is served by Horry County Schools.

How bad is flooding in Conway, and how does it affect a sale?

Flooding is the main risk factor for houses near the Waccamaw River, and Hurricane Florence set the record. The National Weather Service reports the river at Conway crested at a record 21.16 feet in 2018, breaking the Hurricane Matthew crest by more than three feet.

The Horry County emergency plan lists these Waccamaw flood stages:

  • Minor flooding at 11 feet, when roads may be covered.
  • Moderate flooding at 12 feet, when buildings usually begin to flood.

The county plan also notes that the watershed is large and flat, so water can take days to reach the river and stay high for a long time. After Hurricane Florence, nearly 1,000 homes and businesses near the river flooded, and county officials later reported 361 damaged homes in Conway. After Hurricane Joaquin in 2015 and Hurricane Matthew in 2016, hundreds more homes in the county were damaged.

The City of Conway says its riverfront parks are designed to flood, which helps protect private property, and that it changed the electrical boxes in Riverfront Park so they can be removed ahead of rising water. Conway has a humid subtropical climate with mild winters and hot, humid summers. The mean daily high is 58.1 degrees Fahrenheit in January and 90.8 in July, and August is the wettest month at 7.81 inches.

A deed that distributes an estate does not need the usual value affidavit under South Carolina Code section 12-24-70(D), which makes the paperwork lighter than for an ordinary sale. A deed to a mortgagee in lieu of foreclosure is also exempt from the deed recording fee under section 12-24-40.

The heirs still have to agree, and the house still needs a clear title. Horry County records are in the county, so a closing attorney will pull the chain of title before anything is signed.

It can be, since buyers and lenders ask about flood history and insurance. Keep repair records and your flood zone information handy, and ask for a cash offer if repairs are not an option.

Owner-occupied homes are assessed at 4 percent, and non-owner-occupied property at 6 percent. Square footage is taken from exterior measurements, which may differ from the builder's or an agent's figures. If your listing sheet and the county record disagree, that is worth correcting before a buyer notices.

The County Auditor usually mails real property tax bills in September. Tax equals taxable value times the assessment rate times the mill levy divided by 1,000. Local taxing bodies, not the Assessor, set the mill levy, so a bill can rise even when the assessment does not. If your mortgage company pays the taxes, forward any bill you receive to them.

Where is North Augusta, SC, and how is it laid out?

North Augusta sits on the north bank of the Savannah River, directly across the state line from Augusta, Georgia. Most of the city is in western Aiken County, with a small part reaching north into Edgefield County, and it belongs to the Central Savannah River Area and the Augusta metropolitan area.

Because the city straddles two counties, the county that bills your property tax depends on which side of the line the parcel falls. City government is a mayor-council system, with seven council members elected at large to staggered four-year terms, so permit and code questions go to city hall and not the county.

What is North Augusta's history, and why does it matter for a house sale?

North Augusta traces to a land company founded in the 1890s. James U. Jackson and his brother Walter formed the North Augusta Land Company with New York investors, and the company bought a 5,600-acre tract on March 24, 1890. The city was incorporated on April 11, 1906.

The Hampton Terrace Hotel, a resort the Jacksons built, opened in 1903 and burned on December 31, 1916. Much later, the Savannah River Plant was built to the south during the Cold War. The city's population nearly quadrupled, and its area grew from 772 acres to 5,139 acres.

That growth pattern left a mix of early twentieth century streets and postwar subdivisions. The Georgia Avenue and Butler Avenue Historic District is on the National Register of Historic Places, so older homes there may be worth a call to the city before you plan exterior changes.

What do schools, bridges and trails mean for North Augusta buyers?

Most North Augusta students attend Aiken County Public Schools, and the part of the city in Edgefield County is served by the Edgefield County School District. Many families also send children to private schools across the river in Georgia.

  • High schools: North Augusta High School and Fox Creek High School, an independent charter school.
  • Middle schools: North Augusta Middle, Paul Knox Middle and Highland Springs Middle.
  • Elementary schools: Hammond Hill, Belvedere, North Augusta Elementary and Mossy Creek.
  • Greeneway Trail, established in 1995, with more than 9 miles of paved trail on a former railroad line.
  • SRP Park on the Savannah River, home of the Augusta GreenJackets.

The Thirteen Street bridge, also called the James U. Jackson Memorial Bridge, carries traffic across the Savannah River to Augusta. We found no official commute figure, so we do not quote one.

Which counties handle North Augusta property taxes and when are they due?

Aiken County's page says real property bills go out in the fall and are payable without penalty by January 16, with penalties added in January, February and March.

The state code sets the general window from September 30 through January 15 and a penalty sequence of 3, 7 and 5 percent at the dates it lists in Chapter 45. We could not confirm Edgefield County dates from an official page, so owners in that part of the city should ask the Edgefield County offices directly.

Delinquent taxes are referred to the Delinquent Tax Collector, who is in Suite 2500 of the Government Center at 1930 University Parkway in Aiken, and the property can be sold. Aiken County's assessor taxes an owner-occupied home at 4 percent rather than 6 percent of its value, and the owner can claim this on one legal residence in South Carolina. Rental homes, second homes, commercial property and land above five acres may not qualify.

  • Reappraisal increases are capped at 15 percent of the base-year value, using 2007 as that base year.
  • When an assessable transfer occurs, the property's value can be set at current market value instead of being limited by the cap.

In practice, a buyer may see a bigger tax bill than the seller paid. If you are selling, tell the buyer that the figure on your bill may not carry over. The county site did not state an appeal deadline, so call the assessor at the Government Center if you want to challenge a value.

How is a North Augusta deed recorded and what does it cost?

Deeds for North Augusta property in Aiken County are recorded with the Register of Deeds in Suite 2100 of the Government Center, 1930 University Parkway, Aiken. The phone number is 803.642.2072. The office says it does not offer title searches, legal advice or form preparation.

Documents recorded after June 12, 2005 are electronically imaged, but they can be viewed only on computers inside the office, and earlier documents are in books. The county does not publish fee amounts on that page.

South Carolina's deed transfer fee is separate from recording charges. It is $1.85 for each $500 of value, with $1.30 going to the state and $0.55 to the county, according to Chapter 24. Deeds of distribution from an estate are not subject to it, which can help heirs.

Not always. In Aiken County an assessable transfer lets the value reset to current market value instead of being held by the 15 percent cap, so the new bill can rise.

Where is Lexington, SC, and what is the town like?

Lexington is the county seat of Lexington County and the county's most populous town, about 12 miles west of Columbia. It sits in the northeastern part of the county at an elevation of roughly 315 feet.

The town covers about 12 square miles. Fourteenmile Creek drains the north side and Twelvemile Creek the south, and both flow northeast into the Saluda River. Lake Murray lies just north of town, and U.S. Route 1 (Augusta Highway) runs through it.

Wikipedia describes Lexington as a suburb of Columbia, and the town's growth since 2000 follows that pattern. Sellers here usually deal with buyers comparing the lake, the school zone and drive time into Columbia.

What is the history of Lexington, and why does the courthouse town look the way it does?

Lexington began as part of a 1735 colonial township plan, and the name Lexington County replaced Saxe Gotha in 1785 in honor of the battles of Lexington and Concord. Granby was the county seat until chronic flooding moved the courthouse to Lexington in 1820.

The town was incorporated in 1861. Union forces destroyed much of it during the Carolinas campaign, including the courthouse, and fires in 1894 and 1916 led to many of the brick buildings that stand today. Growth picked up with the Columbia to Augusta railroad and the Lexington Textile Mill in the 1890s, then with suburban expansion once cars became common.

The result is a mix of older downtown properties and newer subdivisions. Population went from 9,793 in 2000 to 17,870 in 2010 and 23,568 in 2020. Newer subdivisions sit alongside the older core, so condition varies widely from street to street.

How does Lake Murray affect Lexington property?

Lake Murray is the town's best known feature and it influences nearby property values and buyer interest. The lake was created in 1930 and is held back by a dam about 1.7 miles long, about 5 miles north of town.

The dam roadway is open for driving, biking, running and walking, and a public swimming area operates on the Lexington side in summer. COMET, the Central Midlands Regional Transit Authority, provides public transit. In 2019 SC Highway 6 (Lake Drive) and Church Street became one-way streets downtown, and an overpass across Interstate 20 is a planned project.

The Register of Deeds is at 212 S. Lake Dr., Suite 301, and records deeds, mortgages, liens and plats. Since March 1, 2018, an affidavit is required for taxable or exempt transfers.
